title: Gerrymandering Worked
text:
Republicans got wiped out in the midterms, which means that fears about gerrymandering, diminished Black representation, and the undermining of democracy were all completely overblown. Because Republicans didn’t succeed, nothing was wrong with their efforts.

 Or at least that’s the incorrect conclusion many people are drawing.

 “Last week’s election shattered myriad myths, not least that America is ‘structurally’ racist,” The Wall Street Journal editorialized . “Minority candidates across the country won races up and down the ballot.” Other outlets described the Republican gerrymanders as a “flop” or asserted that they had “ failed ,” while the conservative columnist Quin Hilyer argued that “even after significant post-Callais redistricting, and despite Democrats’ worries, this year’s results showed that Black candidates did just fine.”

 This argument is a little like the episode of The Simpsons in which Sideshow Bob insists on his innocence because: “Attempted murder? Now, honestly, what is that? Do they give a Nobel Prize for attempted chemistry?” Similarly, the idea now is that because attempts to insulate Republican incumbents from democracy and deprive Black voters of political influence failed, no harm was done.

 “Even if the gerrymanders didn’t produce the sort of absolute gains that Republicans had hoped, they absolutely worked in terms of preventing a fair or more proportional change to the status quo,” Justin Levitt, a professor at Loyola Law School, told me. “If you set up a 100-yard dash and you saddle one contestant in the 100-yard dash with running with a 75-pound weighted tie to their ankle, the fact that they may manage to win under extraordinary conditions doesn’t mean that the race looks fair.”

 [ Read: An electoral mess in Missouri ] 

 Democratic voters did overcome some attempts to protect GOP incumbents. They did so by turning out in once-in-a-century numbers against an unpopular president who’d promised no more inflation and no more wars and broken both pledges. If you judge Republican gerrymanders on the basis of whether the GOP kept the House, then you could say that this time, they didn’t work. But they succeeded in both limiting the damage and keeping huge majorities in the delegations of states where Democrats came close to winning or won more than half of the votes. Conversely, Democratic gerrymanders left Republicans with a much lower proportion of seats than their percentage of the vote. A gun doesn’t stop being a lethal weapon just because you miss.

 “Republicans still gained anywhere from four to seven seats as a result of the new maps, even if they didn’t pay off as Republicans hoped,” The New York Times reported in a preliminary analysis last weekend. “If every congressional map had been drawn fairly, with party-blind nonpartisan methods, Democrats might have come close to winning a veto-proof two-thirds majority in the House, with the party winning nearly 20 additional districts in Texas, Florida and Georgia alone.”

 In Texas, Democrats won more than half of the popular vote but netted 14 seats; Republicans won 24, almost twice as many. With a “hypothetical party-blind map, like one drawn by computer simulations,” the Times noted, “Democrats almost certainly would have won a majority of Texas’ House seats.”

 Votes are still being counted, so the numbers remain preliminary. But based on what we know so far, thanks to mid-decade redistricting, only eight of Florida’s 28 congressional districts will go to Democrats, despite Democrats winning about 48 percent of the vote. Eight out of nine congressional districts will go to Republicans in Tennessee, with one close race still uncalled, after Democrats won about 44 percent of the vote. On the Democratic side, California’s gerrymander will leave Republicans with only four seats out of 52, after the GOP won about 30 percent of the vote. Some discrepancy can be explained by political geography—Democratic votes cluster in cities or suburbs while Republican voters are more rural and spread out—but not all of it.

 It is true that some gerrymanders backfired by making the wrong assumptions about the midterm electorate and spreading Republican votes too thin; this happened in Ohio and North Carolina. But the fact that Republicans didn’t succeed in thwarting the will of the electorate does not make the gerrymandering right. Nor do Black voters defying attempts to neutralize their votes by turning out in such huge numbers mean that those attempts were legitimate.

 Even in North Carolina, whose GOP-favorable map has been judged a textbook “dummymander,” Republican lawmakers aren’t clamoring to redraw the map, because they think it will produce the results they want next time. “If any map can withstand a 15-, 20-point swing, it’ll be the first one that I have seen,” Destin Hall, the GOP speaker of the North Carolina House, told reporters . “I’m confident that my party will be able to get back all those congressional seats they lost.” This is as concise a summary as one can get: These gerrymanders failed to thwart the will of so many voters, but in a more normal election, they can be expected to succeed.

 [ Read: Redistricting isn’t going as Republicans planned ] 

 “The harm doesn’t disappear from gerrymandering, from voter suppression and the like, just because people overcame it,” Sophia Lin Lakin, the director of the voting-rights project at the ACLU, told me. “These structures, these maps—they’re gonna be in place for a while.”

 The Journal editorial cites Scott Colom’s victory in Mississippi as evidence that concerns about Black-voter suppression were overblown. A U.S. Senate race by definition cannot be gerrymandered, because senators are elected by statewide popular vote. Never mind that Colom will become the first Black senator from Mississippi in 150 years—the previous one was born enslaved—in a state where nearly half the population is Black.

 A win of this magnitude is unlikely to repeat itself. The question now is whether the parties will realize that trying to disenfranchise their rival constituents is bad for democracy, and be willing to pass federal legislation to prevent it. Unfortunately, at the moment, it seems as though the GOP position is that it just needs to wait for the next election for the lopsided maps to do their work.

 Then there is the particular debt the Democrats owe to Black voters, who powered their wins across the South despite Republicans’ efforts to suppress them. “Black voters have made it abundantly clear that they expect their elected representatives to be looking out for them,” Levitt said. “Along with that comes an expectation, a real firm claim to having voting-rights legislation front and center so that it doesn’t take an extraordinary election with extraordinary turnout in order to produce technical results.”

 Restoring the Voting Rights Act after its virtual nullification by the Supreme Court and imposing some kind of federal limit on partisan gerrymandering would go a long way toward preventing politicians from seeking to disempower voters rather than win them over.
